title: Sea Cows: The Gentle Dugong
summary: How the dugong, a slow sea mammal that grazes on seagrass in the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf, lives, raises its calf, and why it needs protection.
poll: Protecting sea animals like the dugong is everyone's job, not just scientists'.

versions.title: The Sea Cow
versions.text:
A big gray shape swims in the sea. It moves slow. It is a dugong! It is very big. But it is calm.

A dugong is not a fish. It is a mammal. It has to breathe air. So it comes up for air a lot. Then it dives back down. The sea is its home.

Dugongs live in warm seas. Some live near Saudi Arabia. They swim in the Red Sea. They swim in the Gulf, too.

Dugongs eat a sea plant. It is called seagrass. They eat lots of it each day. They eat and eat. A cow eats grass the same way. That is why some call them sea cows!

A dugong is as long as a car. It has a flat tail like a whale. It has two small flippers.

A mom dugong has one baby at a time. The baby is a calf. The calf stays close to its mom. It drinks her milk.

Dugongs are in danger. They get stuck in fish nets. Boats can hit them. Mud and trash hurt the seagrass. We must protect them. Then they can live a long time.

versions.title: Sea Cows: The Gentle Dugong
versions.text:
A large gray animal glides slowly through the clear, warm water. Its round face points down toward the sea floor. This gentle giant is a dugong, and it is one of the most unusual animals in the ocean.

A dugong spends its whole life in the sea, but it is not a fish. It is a mammal, like a camel or a whale. It breathes air, so every few minutes it rises to the surface. It takes a breath through the nostrils on top of its snout, and then it sinks back down.

Dugongs live in warm, shallow waters near the coast. Many of them live near Saudi Arabia, in the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf. The Gulf holds one of the largest groups of dugongs in the world.

Dugongs eat almost nothing but seagrass, a plant that grows on the sandy sea floor. They graze on it slowly, the way cows graze in a field. This is why people call them sea cows. As they feed, they leave long trails in the sand.

An adult dugong is about three meters long. It has a flat tail like a whale's tail, and it also has two short flippers that help it steer.

A mother dugong gives birth to only one calf at a time, and she may wait several years before having another. The calf stays close to her and drinks her milk for more than a year.

Today, dugongs face many threats. They get trapped in fishing nets, and fast boats can hit them. Pollution and coastal building can destroy the seagrass they depend on. Dugongs have very few calves, so it is hard for their numbers to grow back. Many countries, including Saudi Arabia, now protect them by law.

Like all mammals, it breathes air, so every few minutes it rises to the surface, takes a breath through the nostrils on top of its snout, and then sinks quietly back down.

Dugongs inhabit warm, shallow coastal waters in parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Many of them live near Saudi Arabia, in the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, which supports one of the largest dugong populations in the world.

Dugongs eat almost nothing except seagrass, a flowering plant that grows in underwater meadows on the sandy sea floor. Because they graze on it steadily, the way cattle graze in a field, they are often called sea cows. As they feed, they pull up whole plants, roots and all, leaving long, winding trails in the sand.

Today, dugongs face serious threats. They become tangled in fishing nets, and speeding boats can strike them. Pollution and coastal construction destroy the seagrass meadows they depend on. Because dugongs reproduce so slowly, their populations take a long time to recover. For this reason, many countries, including Saudi Arabia, now protect them by law.

versions.title: Sea Cows: The Gentle Dugong
versions.text:
A massive gray animal glides unhurriedly through the warm, transparent water, its rounded face angled toward the sea floor as it searches for its next meal. This gentle giant is a dugong, and although few people have ever seen one, it is among the most remarkable creatures in the ocean.

Although a dugong spends its entire life in the sea, it is not a fish but a marine mammal, and its closest living relatives are the manatee and, surprisingly, the elephant. Like every mammal, it breathes air, so every few minutes it rises to the surface, inhales through the nostrils on top of its snout, and then sinks quietly back toward the bottom.

Dugongs inhabit warm, shallow coastal waters scattered across parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. A significant number live near Saudi Arabia, in the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, and the Gulf supports one of the largest dugong populations in the world.

The dugong is a herbivore that consumes almost nothing except seagrass, a flowering plant that grows in underwater meadows on the sandy sea floor. Because it grazes continuously, much as cattle graze in a pasture, it is frequently called the sea cow. As it feeds, it uproots entire plants, including their roots, leaving long, winding trails across the sand that scientists can follow to learn where dugongs have been feeding.

An adult dugong measures approximately three meters in length and can weigh as much as several adult people combined. Unlike the manatee, which has a rounded, paddle-shaped tail, the dugong has a notched tail similar to a whale's, along with two short flippers that it uses for steering.

A mother dugong gives birth to only one calf at a time, and she may wait several years before producing another. The calf remains beside her and drinks her milk for more than a year, gradually learning where to locate the best seagrass.

Today, dugongs confront serious threats. They become entangled in fishing nets, speeding boats can strike them, and pollution and coastal construction destroy the seagrass meadows on which they depend. Because dugongs reproduce so slowly, their populations require a long time to recover from any losses, and scientists list the species as vulnerable to extinction. Consequently, many countries, including Saudi Arabia, now protect dugongs by law.

versions.title: Sea Cows: The Gentle Dugong
versions.text:
A massive gray animal glides unhurriedly through the warm, transparent water, its rounded, whiskered face angled steadily downward toward the sea floor as it searches methodically for sustenance along the sandy bottom. This gentle giant is a dugong, and although comparatively few people have ever encountered one in the wild during their lifetime, it remains among the most remarkable and genuinely least understood creatures inhabiting the entire ocean today.

Although a dugong spends its entire existence fully submerged in the sea, it is emphatically not a fish but rather a marine mammal, and its closest living relatives are, somewhat surprisingly, the manatee and, quite astonishingly, the elephant, with which it shares a distant common ancestor many millions of years removed in evolutionary time. Like every other mammal on Earth, it requires atmospheric oxygen to survive, so at regular, predictable intervals it ascends patiently to the surface, inhales through nostrils positioned on the upper surface of its snout, and then descends quietly once more toward the seabed far below.

Dugongs inhabit warm, shallow coastal waters distributed across considerable portions of both the Indian and Pacific Oceans. A substantial number reside near Saudi Arabia specifically, within the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, and the Gulf itself supports one of the largest dugong populations found anywhere in the entire world, which confers upon the region a particularly special, almost outsized responsibility for ensuring their continued survival.

The dugong is a herbivore that consumes almost nothing whatsoever except seagrass, a flowering plant that grows in extensive underwater meadows across the sandy sea floor. Because it grazes almost continuously throughout the day, much as cattle graze in an ordinary pasture, it is frequently and affectionately described by many as the sea cow. As it feeds methodically along the bottom, it uproots entire plants, including their nutritious roots, leaving long, meandering trails etched visibly across the sand that researchers can subsequently analyze in detail to determine precisely where dugongs have recently been foraging for food.

An adult dugong measures approximately three meters in length and can weigh as much as several adult humans combined in total mass. Unlike the manatee, which possesses a rounded, paddle-shaped tail, the dugong instead has a distinctly notched tail closely resembling a whale's, accompanied by two short flippers that it uses primarily for steering rather than for generating forward propulsion through the water.

A mother dugong gives birth to only a single calf at any given time, and she may consequently wait several years before ever producing another offspring. The calf remains closely beside her and consumes her milk for well over a full year, gradually learning where to locate the most nourishing seagrass and precisely how to evade dangerous predators such as sharks that patrol the same coastal waters.

Today, dugongs confront numerous significant threats to their continued survival. They frequently become entangled in fishing nets, speeding vessels can strike and seriously injure them, and pollution together with coastal construction steadily destroys the seagrass meadows upon which they entirely and exclusively depend for food. Because dugongs reproduce so remarkably slowly compared with most other mammals, their populations require considerable time to recover from any losses they suffer, and conservation scientists therefore classify the species as vulnerable to extinction. Consequently, numerous countries, including Saudi Arabia, now protect dugongs by law, safeguarding both the animals themselves and the fragile seagrass habitats that ultimately sustain their entire population.

From a distant common ancestor shared improbably with the elephant, millions of years in the past, to a gentle sea cow grazing quietly on meadows across the floor of today's Arabian Gulf, the dugong's entire existence remains tied, generation after generation, inseparably to the health of the seagrass it can never survive without.

MID.prompt: Explain how the dugong's way of life makes it easy to harm. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained at least one reason dugongs are easy to harm.
I used at least two details from the article.
I wrote in complete sentences and checked my spelling.
MID.modelAnswer: A dugong's way of life makes it easy to harm because, as a mammal, it must rise to the surface every few minutes to breathe, which puts it right in the path of speeding boats. It also grazes only on seagrass that grows close to shore, so any threat to that shallow coastal habitat, like pollution or construction, directly threatens the dugong's only food supply too. Because a mother dugong raises just one calf at a time and may wait years before having another, the population recovers extremely slowly whenever these threats take a toll.

HIGH.prompt: Should laws protect seagrass meadows as well as dugongs themselves? Make a claim and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported my claim with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained my reasoning and used correct grammar and punctuation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe laws should protect seagrass meadows just as strongly as they protect the dugongs themselves, because this marine mammal is a herbivore that eats almost nothing else, so losing its food source would be just as deadly as losing the animal directly. The article explains that pollution and coastal construction are already destroying the seagrass meadows that dugongs depend on, which makes this gentle giant especially vulnerable even where hunting or boat strikes are controlled. Because dugongs reproduce so slowly, giving birth to only one calf every few years, a damaged seagrass meadow could take far longer to recover in dugong numbers than in plant growth alone. Protecting the coastal seagrass meadows is really protecting the dugong itself, since one cannot survive for long without the other.
